opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, a lot of it was just the environment I was in at Stanford. I was in Fei-Fei's lab, and Andrej Karpathy was a few desks over. Around 2015 he'd been playing with character-level RNNs, the stuff that became char-rnn and the "Unreasonable Effectiveness of Recurrent Neural Networks" blog post. You'd feed in Shakespeare, or Linux source code, or LaTeX, and this tiny model would spit back text that looked weirdly plausible. It had the right indentation, matched brackets, made-up theorems. That was magical to see at the time.

The question that really grabbed us was: *why* does this work? What is the LSTM actually learning in its hidden state? So we wrote "Visualizing and Understanding Recurrent Networks," where we went inside the cells. We found individual units that tracked things like whether you're inside a quote, or how deep you are in a nested expression, or roughly where you are in a line. These were long-range dependencies, and the gating in LSTMs seemed to be what let them hold onto that information. We also compared against n-gram baselines to see where the gains were really coming from.

On the practical side, I wrote torch-rnn, partly because I wanted a faster, more memory-efficient implementation so people could train these things on a single GPU without much pain. A surprising number of people picked it up for creative projects, which was a lot of fun to watch.

Looking back, it's funny. We were training models with a few million parameters on a few megabytes of text, and you could already see hints of what scaling language models would do. I didn't predict where it would go. I mostly worked on vision and 3D after that. But that period taught me a lot about how much structure a simple next-token objective can pull out of raw data.

r001.rationale: The response says the work asked what LSTMs learned in their hidden states and examined individual units to see what they tracked.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it came out of the lab I was in. I was a PhD student at Stanford with Fei-Fei Li, and Andrej Karpathy and I were sitting a few desks apart. At that point the big story was that convnets had just cracked images, and the obvious question was what the equivalent was for sequences. RNNs had been around forever, but around 2014 and 2015 people were finally training them deep enough and long enough that they actually worked, and LSTMs were the thing that made that stable.

For me it started as a practical need. We were doing image captioning, so we had a convnet on one side producing a vector, and we needed something on the other side that could emit a sentence conditioned on that vector. An LSTM language model was the natural decoder. Once you build one of those, you realize the model doesn't care whether the conditioning is an image or nothing at all, and the unconditional version is just a language model you can sample from.

And sampling from them was genuinely fun. Andrej wrote char-rnn and that blog post about Shakespeare and Linux source code, and I ended up writing torch-rnn partly because char-rnn was slow and memory hungry and I wanted a cleaner, faster implementation. You'd train on a corpus of text overnight on a single GPU and in the morning it would be producing stuff that had the right shape, with balanced braces, plausible variable names, paragraphs that scanned like English even when the content was nonsense. There was no reinforcement learning, no fancy objective, just predicting the next character. The fact that so much structure fell out of that was a hint, and I think a lot of us felt it even if nobody at the time would have extrapolated to where things are now.

The other draw was that it was hands on. The models were small enough that one person could read all the code, understand every gradient, and debug it end to end. That was a nice moment to be a grad student, because the ideas were working but the tooling was still immature enough that building the tooling was itself a contribution.

r001.rationale: The response discusses building and sampling from RNN language models and notes that structure emerged, but it does not describe investigating what their internal neurons were doing.

astra-6.text:
What excited me was the idea that you could treat language as a sequence prediction problem: read some characters or words, predict what comes next, and learn from the text itself. The setup was simple, but it seemed to ask a lot of the model—what could it learn about structure just by doing that?

And there was something really compelling about sampling from these models. You could train an RNN, let it generate text, and get a very immediate feel for what it had picked up and where it fell apart. LSTMs made it possible to explore longer dependencies, so they felt like a really interesting tool for investigating those questions.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses sequence prediction, generated text, and longer dependencies, but does not describe investigating what the models’ internal neurons were doing.

sol-6.1.text: At the time, I was really interested in the intersection of computer vision and language. You had these convolutional networks that were getting very good at recognizing images, and RNNs and LSTMs gave you a way to generate a sequence of words. Putting those together for something like image captioning felt like a really natural next step. It was exciting to move beyond assigning a label to an image and start asking whether a model could describe what was happening in it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses combining vision models with RNNs for image captioning, but does not say the work investigated what the models’ internal neurons were doing.
